title: Global Trends, Local Answers: What Merchants Should Rethink as Payments Get Faster and Smarter
summary: Xendit’s Alicia Vasquez shares takeaways from MRC San Diego 2026: agentic commerce, first-party misuse, Visa’s VAMP threshold, and faster payment rails.
body_markdown:
At MRC San Diego last month,


**Alicia Vasquez, Head of GTM USA at Xendit,** joined payments and fraud leaders for three days of sessions and conversations on where commerce is headed.


MRC San Diego is the Merchant Risk Council's members-only conference for payments and fraud prevention professionals, held from 14 to 16 September at the Hyatt Regency Mission Bay. The conversations kept coming back to two shifts: AI agents entering checkout, and fraud that increasingly starts with a paying customer.


**Alicia's key takeaways:**


- Why agentic commerce strategies built around a card on file won't travel to Southeast Asia


- How first-party misuse and Visa's lower VAMP threshold are changing what merchants need to watch


- Why faster payment rails make local expertise and backup paths more valuable for merchants entering Southeast Asia


## **Small room, big conversations**


I've always been an MRC Vegas girl, but San Diego might have converted me.


This was my first MRC San Diego, and the thing that hit me first was the size. It's members-only and intimate by design, and you could sit down with someone and have a real, in-depth conversation. At Vegas, you say hi, get pulled in five directions, and promise to catch up later. Here, you actually caught up.


I came home with a notebook full of conversations. Here's what stuck.


## **The community is the product**


When I caught up with Julie Ferguson, MRC’s Co-founder and CEO, in San Diego, she said something that stuck with me: MRC wouldn't be what it is without its community.


San Diego drove that home. Whether we were geeking out over agentic commerce, talking about what's next for payments, or sitting in on a fabulous Payments 101 discussion that took us all the way back to basics, the best part was the conversation around it.


Basics matter. Payments people spend so much time on the next shiny thing that we forget how many of our merchants, and our own new hires, are still learning how a card authorization works. Going back to basics is how you bring more people into the room.


## **Agentic commerce went from slideware to strategy**


You couldn't walk ten feet without hearing "agentic." And for good reason:


[63% of merchants are actively exploring or planning to implement agentic AI payments](https://merchantriskcouncil.org/learning/mrc-exclusive-reports/global-payments-and-fraud-report) .


The big open questions are about plumbing. If an AI agent is shopping on someone's behalf, who's liable when something goes wrong? And what does a chargeback even look like when the customer never visited your site?


Here's what I kept bringing up: An agent can only check out with a payment method the shopper has. In Southeast Asia, that's often a QR code, a bank transfer or an e-wallet, and it changes market by market. If your agentic strategy assumes a card on file, you've built it for the Western markets, and this ain't Kansas anymore, honey.


## **The fraudster is sometimes your customer**


This is MRC, so of course we talked fraud. The theme I heard most was first-party misuse: a real, paying customer who's found the dispute button. According to the MRC’s 2026 Global Payments and Fraud Report, 64% of merchants are seeing more of it, and a quarter of them have seen it climb by 25% or more.


That's a harder problem than stolen cards, where there's always a criminal to catch. With first-party misuse, every fix risks turning away someone who did nothing wrong.


The other one keeping people up at night is Visa's VAMP threshold, which dropped from 2.2% to 1.5% on 1 April 2026. A merchant sitting at 1.8% went from compliant to over the line without changing a thing. My takeaway is simple: know your ratio before the network tells you.


## **Faster rails, and why the US playbook doesn't travel**


43% of global merchants now accept real-time local payments. In the US, that still feels like news. In Southeast Asia, it's just how people pay.


Over 60% of all payments in Southeast Asia are now digital. We’ve watched the regional behavior shift from e-wallets toward real-time bank payments and QR codes, and


[national QR standards like Malaysia's DuitNow](https://blog.google/intl/en-my/company-news/around-the-globe/2025_11_e-conomy-sea-report-2025-malaysias/) now work across a growing number of markets.


This is where I see US merchants trip up. They assume the US playbook will work in Southeast Asia and default to the provider they already know. Then they open the box and realize it's a whole other landscape. Payment methods change country to country, and so do the regulators. Even the shopping looks different: it's Shopee, Lazada and TikTok Shop, where back home it's Amazon and Walmart.


Faster money also means less time to catch a bad transaction. That makes your partner's local connections and backup paths matter even more. When something breaks, you want someone on the ground who can fix it in the local language, with the local banks.


## **Payments is a small world**


We partner, compete, teach each other, debate each other, and then inevitably end up together again at another conference in another city.


Thanks, MRC San Diego. Vegas, you may have some competition.
